segments.description: Coaches, our next presenter is Dr Mark Kovacs. Mark is a performance psychologist, researcher, professor, author, speaker and coach with extensive background in training and researching elite athletes. He currently runs a consulting firm focused on optimizing human performance by the practical application of cutting edge science. Today, Mark is going to talk to us about some of the research and design that he has done within the return of serve space. Mark, welcome. Hey everyone, really excited to be chatting about the return of serve. I think we all know outside of the serve, the return of serve is the second most important stroke in the game. And for some players, it may actually be the most important stroke in the game. So the challenge for most of us when we teach and coach the return is there's a lot of variables, the variables predominantly of what is the server doing and where is the server hitting it and then what do we want to do as a returner in response. So you've got all these different variables on every serve. So it's a lot harder, obviously, from a standpoint of teaching and coaching to make it simple for your athletes. So today, what we'd like to chat about is some of the basic premises behind a good return of serve foundation, but then also where the variables are on the return from a movement standpoint that you may want to pay attention to going forward. So when we're thinking the return of serve, we have so many stylistic things.

How someone starts is very individualized to them. You have a walk-up start, you have a deep crouch, you have a relatively upright start, and if you look at some of the best returners, they vary. Most of them have a wide-ish base of support. The wider, the better to an extent. The biggest challenge I see is we look at a Novak Djokovic, for example, unbelievable return of very wide base. You see these 12-year-olds that try to mimic that wide base, and they don't have the strength, they don't have the power, and they can't come out of that wide base as explosively as Novak can. So the big problem we need to do as coaches is be careful about seeing and looking at what the best players in the world do and just assume that a young junior can do that same movement. They don't have that same capability yet. So we have to, you know, graduate that young player to a wider base over time. As their strength levels get better, as their ability to get in and out of their hips improved, and things like that. So it's really important to make sure that it's age and stage appropriate, as you put this sort of technical model in for how does an athlete return. So the start, obviously, is a priority, need to get it right, need to work on it from a comfort standpoint. But also be really careful that you try to impose a start that you visually like that may not fit the athlete's personality or body or physical limitations.
